title: Programmable living medicines that sense and respond inside the body

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a living treatment made from engineered cells or microbes that detects a clinically meaningful signal inside the body and responds by producing or releasing a therapeutic substance. Its defining capability is dependable coupling between sensing and treatment: the biological system must recognize when intervention is appropriate, deliver a useful response, and remain controllable as conditions change.

Conceptual synthesis: a complete system would combine a biological sensor, a decision mechanism, a therapeutic output, and a way to stop activity or clear the engineered organisms. Control could be biological, externally commanded, or shared between organisms and a device. An externally triggered response would demonstrate a different capability from autonomous recognition and treatment of disease; either architecture would need to establish how its sensing actually governs therapeutic action.

The intended breakthrough is a reliable therapeutic system, including safe termination, despite variation between patients, changing disease states, and possible biological drift. This places the concept at the intersection of synthetic biology, biomedical engineering, bioelectronics, therapeutic delivery, and clinical medicine.

significance.text: Conditional significance: a dependable living medicine could respond to a changing pathological state and generate treatment near the site where it is needed. If sensing and therapeutic output tracked disease activity accurately, treatment could adapt over time instead of depending entirely on a predetermined dosing schedule. Better disease control or reduced exposure elsewhere in the body would be potential benefits requiring direct clinical evidence.

A reusable engineering platform could make responsive treatments possible across several diseases. That possibility depends on more than exchanging one sensor or therapeutic payload: each application would require validation of signal interpretation, delivery, response strength, safety, and clinical benefit. Success in one organism, anatomical location, or disease would establish a bounded capability rather than broad platform generality.

Conceptual limit: describing such a treatment as a medicine that monitors and adjusts itself is useful only if the system demonstrates both functions and their reliable connection. Local production alone does not establish appropriate dosing, and detection of an inflammation-related signal does not establish that the signal identifies when treatment will help. External supervision may remain part of a successful design, with corresponding limits on autonomy and practical use.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability identified by the supplied concept is reliable integration of clinically relevant sensing, appropriate therapeutic action, continued control, and safe termination inside a variable biological environment. The supplied evidence does not establish how close existing systems are to satisfying that complete requirement or whether it remains unmet in every narrower application.

Engineering analysis: the sensing mechanism must distinguish actionable disease activity from normal variation and unrelated signals. The response mechanism must turn that information into a suitable therapeutic dose with an appropriate onset and duration. Important design questions include false activation, missed activation, response delays, excessive output, and whether treatment changes the sensed signal in ways that destabilize subsequent responses.

Engineering analysis: living components must retain their intended behavior over the period of use. Relevant barriers include variation in survival and activity between patients, changes in the local biological environment, and biological drift that could weaken sensing, alter output, or bypass control mechanisms. Delivery to the intended location, persistence for the desired duration, and interactions with the host would also need application-specific evaluation.

Engineering analysis: stopping therapeutic production and clearing engineered organisms are separate requirements. A system could cease producing its payload while organisms remain present, or organisms could be removed while a previously released payload continues acting. Designs that use an ingestible device or another external controller would additionally need dependable communication and defined behavior when commands, power, or sensing information are unavailable.

current_state.text: The supplied research reports a proof of concept dated 28 July 2025 under the title “Ingestible optoelectronic capsules enable bidirectional communication with engineered microbes for controllable therapeutic interventions,” with DOI 10.1038/s41564-025-02057-w. It describes engineered E. coli combined with an ingestible optoelectronic capsule and smartphone control, inflammation-related sensing, and light-triggered production or secretion of an anti-inflammatory nanobody in pigs. These details are retained as the research’s account of a reported experiment; the supplied review could not verify them from the retained source.

The access limitation materially constrains interpretation. According to the validated review, the retained PubMed artifact contains only a cookie-access notice, with no inspectable abstract, methods, results, author list, or publication date. Although the source index records a saved, nontruncated HTML artifact with 153 extracted characters, that describes the retained notice and does not establish successful capture or completeness of the intended scientific document. The review therefore could not independently confirm the article’s identity or experimental details.

The earlier research says that a first pass inspected the abstract and that the publisher page failed to open. That account of earlier access cannot itself be substantiated by the retained artifact. The evidence gap does not show that the reported experiment is false; it means the supplied review cannot establish its results, publication status, methods, or strength of evidence.

Even if the reported pig experiment is confirmed, the description would establish a bounded animal proof of concept involving externally triggered therapeutic output. It would not by itself establish autonomous treatment decisions, durable function, safe clearance, or improved outcomes in humans. The supplied account also does not resolve whether inflammation sensing directly controlled treatment or was demonstrated alongside a separately commanded response.

The review reports an empty freshness record, so these materials do not establish the broader state of the field as of 1 November 2026. They support neither a conclusion that a general autonomous, durable human therapy has been achieved nor a comprehensive conclusion that no such therapy exists. No independently inspectable human trial outcomes, durability measurements, or clearance results are supplied.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: controlled human studies should establish the complete chain from detection of a specified disease signal to a measured therapeutic response and improved clinical outcomes. Evaluation should distinguish sensor performance, therapeutic output, and patient benefit so that successful activity at one stage is not mistaken for successful operation of the whole system. Comparators and endpoints should fit the disease and intended clinical use.
completion_criteria.label: Controlled human studies demonstrate signal-triggered treatment improves clinical outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reliability criteria: studies should define disease-appropriate operating durations and measurable limits for false activation, missed activation, response delay, output variability, and loss of function. Extended observation should test whether performance persists as disease activity and biological conditions change. The supplied materials provide no numerical thresholds; acceptable boundaries would need to be specified and justified for each application.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained sensing and treatment meet justified application-specific reliability limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed control and termination criteria: demonstrate that external intervention can predictably reduce or stop therapeutic production, and separately establish whether engineered organisms can be cleared within a defined period. Measurements should distinguish residual organisms, residual therapeutic activity, and any need for additional treatment. Testing should include foreseeable failures of biological control and, where applicable, device communication.
completion_criteria.label: External intervention predictably controls production, with organism clearance separately assessed

completion_criteria.text: Proposed platform criteria: reproducible results across patient groups, manufacturing batches, and independent clinical settings would strengthen confidence in reliability. Successful controlled trials across multiple diseases would provide stronger evidence of modular reuse, but this is a chosen platform-level test rather than a necessary definition of success for a single useful medicine. Finite demonstrations establish the breadth actually tested, not universal programmability.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Reproducible controlled trials across diseases demonstrate modular reuse

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BME-18, “Long-lived continuous sensing of multiple clinically useful biomarkers,” overlaps with the sensing component. BME-05 additionally requires sensing to govern therapeutic action and includes control of the living treatment. BME-07, “A broadly effective early-warning test for lethal cancers,” also depends on clinically meaningful signals, but its central outcome is early detection rather than an ongoing therapeutic response inside the body.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-02, “Programmable delivery of genetic therapies to most tissues,” shares challenges of delivery, targeting, and biological specificity. Its defining goal concerns access to tissues for genetic intervention; BME-05 concerns sustained behavior of engineered living components that sense and respond. Genetic delivery could help construct or deploy a living medicine without establishing its subsequent reliability.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-08, “Reliable, antigen-specific immune tolerance,” could overlap with an application in which living medicines regulate immune activity. Responsive production of an anti-inflammatory agent would not by itself demonstrate antigen-specific tolerance. BME-11, “Controlled regeneration of complex organs in the adult body,” could likewise use responsive biological signals, but successful drug production would not establish organized regeneration of a functional organ.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-13, “Durable autonomous artificial-organ replacement,” shares the goal of sustained therapeutic function with limited intervention, while BME-16, “Long-lived tissue-integrated interfaces for implants,” shares concerns about durable interaction with the body when a device is involved. BME-05 does not inherently require whole-organ replacement or a tissue-integrated implant. The bidirectional communication suggested by the reported capsule concept is also distinct from BME-04’s bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation.

Roster-based synthesis: BME-10, “Validated patient-specific models for testing treatments before use,” could support prediction and testing of living-medicine behavior, while BME-15, “Accessible deep-body molecular imaging,” could help observe location or activity. Neither predictive modeling nor observation alone establishes dependable sensing, therapeutic response, and termination within the patient.

unresolved_issues: The intended article’s identity, authors, publication date, publication status, and full scientific content remain independently unverified within the supplied review.

The retained artifact cannot substantiate the reported E. coli, smartphone control, inflammation sensing, nanobody secretion, or pig experiments; the earlier claim of abstract inspection also remains unverified.
Whether the reported experiment coupled sensed inflammation to therapeutic activation, rather than demonstrating sensing and externally commanded output separately, remains unclear.
Experimental performance, therapeutic benefit, dose control, duration, biological stability, adverse effects, and clearance outcomes cannot be assessed from the supplied artifact.
The materials do not establish field-wide progress or the availability of durable autonomous human therapies as of 1 November 2026.
Disease-specific operating durations and acceptable sensing, response, shutdown, and clearance thresholds remain to be proposed and justified.

brief.title: Living medicines that sense when treatment is needed
possible: People could receive living treatments that detect disease signals inside the body and make medicine where it is needed. Engineered cells or microbes would adjust their activity as conditions change, with a dependable way to stop treatment and clear them.
why: For people with changing disease activity, treatment could follow what their body needs instead of relying entirely on a fixed dosing schedule. Producing medicine near the affected tissue could improve disease control and reduce exposure elsewhere in the body.

sources.showed: Engineered bacteria detected an inflammation signal in pigs and reported it through a swallowable electronic capsule. Smartphone commands triggered light that made the bacteria release a protein treatment to ease bowel inflammation.
sources.quote: This signal is transduced by the optoelectronic capsule into a wireless electrical signal and remotely monitored by a smartphone.
sources.cited_for: The study connects inflammation sensing with electronic monitoring and externally controlled treatment in pigs.
sources.not_established: It does not establish autonomous treatment decisions, lasting reliability, safe clearance or benefit in humans.

sources.showed: Engineered mammalian cells automatically responded to inflammation signals by producing treatment proteins. Implanted cells reduced bowel disease in mice, and an external chemical signal could reset the system.
sources.quote:
The microencapsulated anti-in ﬂammatory device
signiﬁcantly reduced the pathology in dextran sodium sulfate
(DSS)-induced acute murine colitis, demonstrating a synthetic
immunological approach for autonomous anti-in ﬂammatory
therapy.
sources.cited_for: The study demonstrates automatic sensing linked to treatment in mice, with an external reset mechanism.
sources.not_established: It does not establish durable treatment in humans or safe removal of the engineered cells.

sources.showed: Engineered bacteria detected an inflammation-related chemical in mouse guts for 6 months. They retained a biological memory of exposure that researchers could read through stool testing.
sources.quote:
Here we 
report stable, engineered bacterial strains that maintain their function for 6 months in the mouse 
gut.
sources.cited_for: The study shows that engineered bacteria can retain a sensing function during prolonged residence in the gut.
sources.not_established: It demonstrates detection rather than treatment, and does not establish lasting therapeutic control in humans.

shown: Animal studies demonstrate different parts of the capability. Roman Jerala and collaborators built implanted cells that automatically sensed inflammation and reduced bowel disease in mice. Xinyu Zhang and collaborators combined bacterial sensing with a swallowable capsule and smartphone-controlled treatment in pigs.

David T Riglar and collaborators demonstrated bacterial sensing that lasted 6 months in mouse guts. Together, these results establish animal examples of responsive treatment, external control and lasting detection.
missing: Controlled human studies still need to connect disease detection, appropriate medicine production and improved health.
Combined sensing and treatment must stay reliable as disease activity and conditions inside the body change.
External intervention must reliably stop production, while clearance of engineered organisms and lingering medicine is assessed separately.

milestones.label: Signal-triggered treatment improves health in controlled human studies
milestones.explanation: Controlled human studies would have to link a specified disease signal to treatment production and better clinical outcomes. This would establish benefit from the complete system.

milestones.label: Sensing and treatment remain reliable throughout use
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to meet justified limits on false alarms, missed signals, delays and treatment output over the intended duration. This would establish dependable operation as conditions change.

milestones.label: External control stops production, with clearance assessed separately
milestones.explanation: External intervention would have to predictably reduce or stop production, with organism clearance and lingering treatment effects assessed separately. This would establish control when treatment needs to end.

milestones.label: Controlled trials reproduce success across diseases
milestones.explanation: Controlled trials would have to reproduce benefits across diseases, patient groups, production batches and independent clinical settings. This would support reuse beyond a single useful treatment.

uncertain: Which disease signals reliably identify when treatment will help, rather than merely indicating inflammation?
What limits on errors, response time, duration and clearance are acceptable for each disease?
How much external supervision will each treatment need to remain dependable?

page.title: Sense-and-respond living therapeutics
page.definition: Engineered cells or microbes sense a disease-associated signal inside a patient and use a synthetic gene circuit—a linked set of genes implementing control—to regulate production or release of a therapeutic molecule. The signal governs the therapeutic output.

goal.need: ARPA-H cites estimates that up to 50% of U.S. adults do not take medicines as directed, causing more than US$100 billion in preventable annual costs. Its REACT programme pursues cell-based delivery and biomarker monitoring. EBRC separately calls for cells that connect environmental sensing to therapeutic release; clinical benefit remains a product-specific question.

figures.caption: Medication non-adherence estimates cited by ARPA-H
rows: U.S. adults not taking medicines as directed
figures.note: These are programme-cited estimates, not measured benefits of living therapeutics.

statements.quote: Human or human microbiota chassis that can sense and respond with therapeutics release to a range of relevant environmental conditions at clinically relevant concentrations.
statements.context: A milestone in the Space Health roadmap; chassis means the host cells carrying the engineered circuit.

statements.body: Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health
statements.quote: Establishing reliable and accurate release of the therapy or accurate tracking of a biomarker for at least one year after implantation.
statements.context: REACT sets this duration for its separate Living Pharmacy and Living Sentinel tracks; the statement does not require autonomous coupling between them.

completion.title: FDA licenses a living medicine whose engineered circuit couples an internal disease signal to treatment.
completion.criterion: FDA issues a biologics licence for a specified human indication to a product whose documented engineered circuit couples an in-body disease-associated signal to therapeutic-molecule production or release. The biological product and its manufacture meet applicable safety, purity and potency requirements. Licensure applies to the particular product and indication.
completion.set_by: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, general biologic licensing requirements in 21 CFR 601.2 and 601.4.
completion.threshold_quote: the establishment(s) and the product meet applicable requirements to ensure the continued safety, purity, and potency of such products.
completion.basis: Licensure supplies an external clinical and manufacturing decision for a defined medicine. FDA's general standard is applied here to a product with an engineered signal-to-output mechanism; it is not a dedicated circuit-performance standard. No qualifying licence was identified in the searched FDA approval records.

milestones.title: A living medicine establishes preclinical proof of concept for its signal-to-treatment mechanism.
milestones.criterion: Preclinical studies establish feasibility and the proposed biological mechanism, including effective dose range and delivery. Mammalian cells: Smole et al. (2017) demonstrated endogenous inflammatory activation in mice, with five mice per group; their colitis efficacy experiment instead used injected human cytokines. Microbes: Zhang et al. (28 July 2025) demonstrated nitric-oxide sensing and smartphone-triggered nanobody release in pigs, with three biological replicates in the reported colitis assays. The pig result supports supervised delivery, not autonomous disease-triggered treatment.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 2013 preclinical guidance, section III.B.4, written for cellular and gene therapy products; the general pharmacology requirement for investigational drugs is in 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8).
milestones.threshold_quote: establish the feasibility and rationale for use of an investigational CGT product in the targeted patient population.

milestones.title: A living medicine has pharmacology and toxicology evidence supporting reasonably safe human exposure.
milestones.criterion: Pharmacology and toxicology support reasonably safe exposure in the proposed human investigation. Component results are narrower: Riglar et al. (2017) recovered functional sensing bacteria after 200 days from three donor mice, without a therapeutic payload. Smole et al. (2017) reduced mouse circuit output to about 20% after 48 hours using doxycycline, with four mice per group. Zhang et al. (2025) assessed capsule biosafety in three pigs over two four-day administrations. These results do not establish a complete product safety package.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8), pharmacology and toxicology information supporting an investigational new drug application.
milestones.threshold_quote: it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations.

milestones.title: A living medicine enters human testing under an effective investigational new drug application.
milestones.criterion: Human participants receive the product under an effective investigational new drug application: normally 30 days after FDA receipt without a clinical hold, or earlier FDA notification. Microbes: Synlogic reported FDA clearance of SYNB1891's application in 2019; its study treated 32 adults with advanced cancers, 24 alone and eight with atezolizumab, between December 2019 and December 2021. Mammalian cells: E-SYNC's sponsor describes a phase I glioblastoma study with planned enrollment of 20, without a final treated count.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.40, conditions for administering an investigational drug to human participants.
milestones.threshold_quote: An investigator may not administer an investigational new drug to human subjects until the IND goes into effect

milestones.title: A living medicine yields human dose and pharmacology data sufficient to design phase II studies.
milestones.criterion: Phase I establishes pharmacology and dose-related adverse effects sufficiently to design controlled phase II studies. SYNB1891's protocol targeted approximately 30% dose-limiting toxicity during the first 21-day cycle to identify its maximum tolerated dose. Among 32 treated participants, one had dose-limiting grade 3 cytokine-release syndrome at 3 × 10^8 live cells; neither a maximum tolerated nor recommended phase II dose was determined. E-SYNC specifies safety and tissue-priming objectives; its sponsor record supplies no completed endpoint results.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(a). The numerical dose-finding target is specific to Synlogic's SYNB1891 protocol, version 4, dated 27 July 2020; it is not a class-wide toxicity threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: sufficient information about the drug's pharmacokinetics and pharmacological effects should be obtained to permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies.

milestones.title: A living medicine demonstrates substantial evidence of effectiveness for its proposed human indication.
milestones.criterion: Adequate and well-controlled clinical evidence establishes effectiveness for the proposed indication, with disease-specific endpoints and analyses. FDA can consider one investigation plus confirmatory evidence sufficient; its June 2026 revised draft discusses this route and is not binding guidance. This is the clinical-evidence stage before the licensing decision, which also evaluates safety and manufacturing. The cited studies do not establish this stage for either cell type.
milestones.set_by: FDA's substantial-evidence standard for biologic effectiveness, described in sections II and IV of its June 2026 revised draft guidance; the draft is not a binding requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: FDA has also generally considered substantial evidence of effectiveness to be necessary to support licensure of a biological product

not_found: No dedicated clinical completion standard or class-wide numerical limits for sensing errors, response latency, functional lifetime and organism clearance were found in FDA guidance, EBRC roadmaps or REACT materials.
No FDA licence for a product meeting the defined engineered signal-to-treatment capability was identified.
The 2026 E-SYNC conference abstract could not be opened; the accessible sponsor record does not supply completed endpoint results.
The capsule article's abstract and extended-data legends were accessible, but its main methods and results remained behind subscription access.

results.finding: Engineered E. coli released an anti-inflammatory nanobody to alleviate colitis in pigs; sample size not reported.
results.detail: Nitric oxide sensing signaled inflammation, but treatment was activated by a smartphone-controlled LED. The excerpt does not establish an effective dose range or autonomous disease-triggered treatment.
results.quote: Smartphone wireless signals activate LED irradiation in the optoelectronic capsule, in turn activating the microbial expression and secretion of an anti-inflammatory nanobody to alleviate colitis in pigs.

results.finding: Implanted mammalian cell circuit responded to endogenous inflammation in mice; n = 4 for therapeutic-output assays.
results.detail: The circuit produced therapeutic proteins after endogenous inflammation, and reduced colitis pathology after injection of human cytokines. The study did not establish an effective therapeutic dose range.
results.quote:
Similarly as described
above (Figure 4F), we have shown autonomous in vivo activation of
the device by the CLP procedure, detected by anti-inﬂammatory ther-
apeutics 72 hr post-implantation ( Figure 5D).

results.finding: Doxycycline reduced implanted circuit activity to around 20% after 48 hours in mice; n = 4.
results.detail: The externally controlled shutdown is a safety-related component result, but it does not establish pharmacology and toxicology sufficient for reasonably safe human exposure.
results.quote:
Additionally, when mIL-10, which
has a short serum half-life (approximately 2 hr 38), was monitored, we
demonstrated that one injection of Dox 24 hr after the system activa-
tion (thin arrow in Figure 6D) decreased the activity of fully activated
system to around 20% after 48 hr ( Figures 6D and S6D).

results.finding: Engineered E. coli detected tetrathionate in 8 of 9 IL10-deficient mice.
results.detail: The experiment supports disease-associated signal sensing, but the bacteria were diagnostic and did not produce or release a therapeutic molecule.
results.quote:
The engineered bacteria (≥3 measurements over ≥2-weeks) detected 
tetrathionate in 8/9 IL10−/− mice, but not in separately-reared retired C57Bl/6 breeder 
controls (Fig. 2e).

results.finding: E. coli recovered from 3 donor mice retained sensing function after 200 days of colonization.
results.detail: Long-term circuit function is relevant to product stability, but the bacteria carried no therapeutic payload and the study did not establish a pharmacology and toxicology package for human exposure.
results.quote:
In 
vivo function was further confirmed through administration of PAS638 and S. typhimurium 
ΔttrR to C57Bl/6 mice (n=5 per group), using PAS638 colonies isolated after colonization of 
three separate 129X1/SvJ mice for 200 days.

results.finding: Engineered mammalian-cell implants reduced arthritis clinical scores by 40% in mice (n=20 treated; n=12 and 8 controls).
results.detail: Subcutaneous implants responded to inflammation; a separate luciferase reporter demonstrated in vivo response dynamics. Eight therapeutic scaffolds mitigated clinical severity, while four did not significantly do so.
results.quote: Animals receiving Ccl2-IL1Ra implants demonstrated significant amelioration of arthritis severity, including 40% reductions in both clinical scores and ankle thickness, compared to control animals that received Ccl2-Luc constructs or no implant (

results.finding: In a glioblastoma xenograft study, all 6 mice given synNotch-CAR T cells achieved complete, long-term tumor remission.
results.detail: Tumor-antigen sensing induced CAR expression, and intravenous delivery produced antitumor activity. The study compared two cell doses, but the supplied text does not establish an effective dose range; it describes the lower dose as suboptimal.
results.quote: In notable contrast, all of the mice treated with the synNotch-CAR T cells showed complete and long-term remission of the GBM6 tumors.

results.finding: Engineered E. coli Nissle improved colitis measures in mice; 10 mice per group.
results.detail: Orally delivered bacteria used a zinc-responsive circuit to produce IL-10, and sensor activation depended on calprotectin in a separate mouse experiment. The therapeutic experiment tested one bacterial dose, so it did not establish an effective dose range.
results.quote: These data show that both systems can sense intestinal inflammation and resolve inflammation by production of an anti‐inflammatory protein.

results.finding: Glucose-responsive probiotics improved glycaemic control in diabetic mice and monkeys; a three-dose mouse study used n=4 mice.
results.detail: The paper describes oral delivery and glucose-regulated therapeutic expression. The provided text lists the doses tested but does not report which doses were effective, so it does not establish an effective dose range.
results.quote: We show efficacy from the engineered probiotics for glycaemic control in multiple diabetic mouse and non-human primate models, demonstrating that long-term oral administration drives clear improvements in lipid profiles, while also attenuating development of multiple diabetic complications.

results.finding: Inducible IL-12–engineered TILs were administered to 33 patients with metastatic melanoma.
results.detail: The paper reports human treatment but does not state whether it occurred under an effective investigational new drug application.
results.quote: Thirty-three patients with metastatic melanoma were treated in a cell dose escalation trial of autologous TILs transduced with a gene encoding a single-chain IL12 driven by a nuclear factor of the activated T cells promoter (NFAT. IL12).

results.finding: GD2IL18CART phase I (n=23) established recommended doses; one patient had fatal dose-limiting hyperinflammation.
results.detail: The study reported cell expansion, cytokine kinetics and dose-related toxicity. Recommended doses were 2 × 10^5 CAR-positive T cells/kg for children and 1 × 10^5/kg for adults, providing a basis for phase II dosing. Dose-extension cohorts remain ongoing.
results.quote: Following joint review with the DMC, the investigators decided not to pursue further dose escalation despite the absence of formal DLTs at DL1.25, given the risk of life-threatening inﬂammatory toxicity. Consequently, the recommended dose was established at DL1.25 for pediatric patients and DL1 for adults.

results.finding: In 32 participants treated with SYNB1891, one experienced dose-limiting cytokine-release syndrome.
results.detail: The dose-limiting event was grade 3 cytokine-release syndrome at 3 × 10^8 live cells. The study observed pharmacodynamic activity, but neither a maximum tolerated dose nor a recommended phase II dose was determined.
results.quote: Five cytokine release syndrome events occurred with monotherapy, including one that met the criteria for dose-limiting toxicity at the highest dose; no other SYNB1891-related serious adverse events occurred, and no SYNB1891-related infections were observed.
